title: Sampled trace instrumentation diary — lightweight per-request profiling
content:
Purpose:
Lightweight approach to collect per-request microtraces from the serving runtime without adding significant overhead to hot paths. Want to capture root causes of p99 spikes during bursty ingress while keeping global overhead <2%.

Background / motivation:
- Full-coverage tracing is too expensive (CPU + network and storage) when running at production QPS.
- We already have metrics histograms and tail alerts, but lack causal traces to understand where time is spent (scheduler queuing vs token-generation vs kernel stalls).
- Hypothesis: adaptive sampled traces triggered by simple anomaly-detectors will yield high-value traces during incidents while staying cheap in steady state.

Experiment summary (iterations):
1) Baseline: 0.1% uniform sampling of full traces (existing tracer).
   - Overhead measured: +0.6% CPU, network tail opaque but storage growth ~+12%/day.
   - Captured about 1 in 1000 requests; insufficient coverage for rare tail patterns (microbursts, cache-miss cascades).
2) Adaptive sampler prototype (this diary): 0.5% base + burst-bump to 5% for 2 minutes when anomaly detected by sliding-window p99 > baseline*1.6 or request queuing > 10ms.
   - Implemented in-serving: very low-code change, detector uses rolling-exponentially-weighted quantiles from in-memory metrics.
3) Heuristic add-ons: include header-based sticky-sampling for long-lived sessions and backoff suppression for noisy tenants.

Test harness (production shadow):
- Time window: 10 days (2025-11-01 to 2025-11-10) in shadow cluster (dedicated small fleet).
- Traffic: 30% sampled copy of real ingress; mixture of bursty and steady customers.
- Configs: model = llama-2-13b-quant-v2; seq len distribution mean=128 tokens, 99th=1024; average QPS=450 across fleet.

Instrumentation details:
- Trace capture points: ingress queue timestamp, pre-scheduler dequeue, kernel-launch, kv-cache lookup hit/miss, token-emit timing, network flush.
- Payloads: only timing spans + categorical tags (tenant id hash truncated, model id, route); no user content.
- Storage: compressed trace bundles into per-hour blobs in S3 (TTL 7d for sampled, 30d for anomaly-window traces).

Key results (aggregated):
- Effective trace volume: base 0.5% => ~3.4K traces/day; bump windows added ~12K traces/day on days with 2+ bursts. Net storage + processing cost ~+18% vs baseline metrics-only.
- Overhead on p50 latency: +0.3ms avg (statistically insignificant).
- CPU overhead: +1.4% at node-level during steady state; spikes to +2.8% during sustained bump windows (acceptable).
- Coverage: captured 82% of p99 incidents (as flagged by metrics) with at least one trace in the 2-minute window. Baseline 0.1% captured ~19%.

Representative trace archetypes discovered:
A) Kernel-saturation sequence: long kernel queue -> multiple token stalls -> compounded kv-cache lookup bursts. Mostly on older GPU types during multi-tenant noisy periods.
B) Scheduler-fanout delay: ingress queue starves one CPU thread causing head-of-line delay for small requests (short sequences).
C) KV-cache cold-miss cascade: miss at shard leader leads to synchronous fetch that blocks next tokens; pattern appears with specific tenant embeddings usage.

Actionable takeaways:
- Adaptive bumping recovered most useful traces for diagnosis with modest cost.
- Kernel-saturation traces point to a need for per-GPU priority lanes or soft-reservation for small requests on heterogeneous fleets.
- Scheduler delays indicate an opportunity to change thread-pool sizing and to add a short-term preemption for tiny requests.
- KV-cache misses suggest evaluating a small L1 in-host cache for hot tenant embeddings.

Risks / privacy notes:
- Traces contain tenant IDs (hashed) and model identifiers only; confirm legal ok with privacy/compliance (opened ENG-PRIV-102).
- Storage TTLs must be enforced to avoid drift into long-term archival.

Open questions / next experiments:
1) Smarter anomaly detection: use lightweight ML classifier on metrics stream to trigger bump (goal: reduce bump volume by 25% while keeping recall >0.8).
2) Dynamic bump length: extend bump if consecutive anomalies observed, otherwise decay faster than 2 minutes.
3) Tenant-aware sampling: increase base sample for high-value tenants (product experiments) to avoid always relying on bumps.
4) Synthetic fuzzing: inject microburst patterns in canary to validate pipeline end-to-end and ensure no trace-loss in our collector.

Immediate next steps (short checklist):
- [ ] Add backoff suppression for noisy test tenants (complete prototype).
- [ ] Create dashboard: traces-per-hour, bump-frequency, cost-estimate per bump (WIP PR linked).
- [ ] Run controlled canary with synthetic 10x microbursts on staging fleet (scheduled 2026-03-05).
- [ ] Draft runbook: how to pull relevant traces during incidents and correlate with SLO alert windows.

Misc notes / rough numbers for on-call reference:
- Sampling config: base=0.5%, bump=5%, bump-trigger: rolling-p99>1.6x baseline or queue>10ms, bump-ttl=120s.
- Observed mean time-to-first-trace-after-spike: ~22s (detector + bump delay).
- False bump rate: ~0.9 bumps/day per 100k requests (acceptable).

If we adopt this approach more widely, we should:
- Standardize trace schema (span names + tags) and maintain minimal versioned contract.
- Add a low-cost cross-tenant index to find traces quickly by approximate time + tenant-hash.
- Evaluate integrating traces with existing flame-graph generator for kernel stalls.

Notes to self:
- Keep collector stateless where possible; avoid adding long-lived dependencies into serving hot path.
- Re-check privacy with legal before expanding retention.

References / links:
- Telemetry PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/telemetry/pull/142
- Incident example (metrics-only): JIRA-INC-3273
- Design sketch: /confluence/tracing/adaptive-sampling (draft)

End of diary entry.
summary: Diary of an adaptive sampled-trace experiment: 0.5% base + 5% bump on anomaly. Captured 82% of p99 incidents with ~+1.4% CPU overhead; revealed kernel saturation, scheduler fanout delays, and kv-cache cold-miss cascades. Next: smarter detector, tenant-aware sampling, and canary fuzzing.
